title: Seasonal Dynamics of Honeybee Forage Plants and Floral Phenology Reveal Critical Forage Gaps in Tigray, Ethiopia
content: This study assessed honeybee forage plant diversity, seasonal phenology, and beekeepers’ knowledge of forage resources and flowering calendars in selected zones of Tigray, Ethiopia. A cross-sectional survey using multistage sampling included 378 households from the Southern, Southeastern, and Eastern Zones. Data were collected through questionnaires, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions. Respondents identified 82 honeybee forage species belonging to 22 families, including 37 herbaceous species, 27 trees, and 18 shrubs, with Fabaceae, Asteraceae, and Lamiaceae among the dominant families. Forage resources showed pronounced seasonal variation in flowering richness, growth form complementarity, and nectar and pollen availability. Flowering richness ranged from 10 species in February to 38 in September. The forage gap index was highest in February (0.737), January (0.632), and March (0.553), identifying January–March as the critical forage dearth period, whereas September–November was resource rich. Nectar and pollen richness peaked in September. Age, education, and family size significantly influenced beekeepers’ forage knowledge, while education predicted flowering-calendar knowledge. Deforestation, agricultural expansion, and fuelwood production were major threats. Conserving diverse native forage plants and strengthening seasonal management are essential for sustaining floral resources and honeybee productivity in seasonally variable agroecosystems.
